tutorials.content:
Let's compute the first few powers of $\textrm{i},$ where $\textrm{i} = \sqrt{-1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{i}}^{0} & =1 \\ {\text{i}}^{1} & =\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{2} & =-1 \\ {\text{i}}^{3} & ={\text{i}}^{2}\cdot \text{i}=(-1)\cdot \text{i}=-\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{4} & ={\text{i}}^{2}\cdot {\text{i}}^{2}=(-1)\cdot (-1)=1\end{aligned}
$$

We can use these results to evaluate expressions containing powers of $\textrm{i}.$ Let's take a look at some examples.

tutorials.name: The Cyclic Nature of Powers of i
tutorials.problem:
Let's remind ourselves of the first few powers of $\textrm{i}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{i}}^{1} & =\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{2} & =-1 \\ {\text{i}}^{3} & =-\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{4} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

At the fourth power, we return to the value of $1,$ which can also be written as $\textrm{i}^0 = 1.$ This means that if we continue to increase the powers, we would cycle through the same four values once again, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14199584/assets/5e3f3a42dd591daf109e474eec99e446706e0d8e46f1252540839cd50d957463.png)

So, for $\textrm{i}^5$ through $\textrm{i}^8,$ the exact same pattern repeats. Remembering that $\textrm{i}^4 = 1,$ we have

$$
\eqalign{
		\textrm{i}^5&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i} &= \textrm{i}\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^6&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^2 &=-1\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^7&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^3 &= -\textrm{i} \[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^8&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^4 &= 1 .
	}
$$

Similarly, for $\textrm{i}^9$ through to $\textrm{i}^{12},$ the pattern repeats again:

$$
\eqalign{
		\textrm{i}^9&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i} &= \textrm{i}\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^{10}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^2 &=-1\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^{11}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^3 &= -\textrm{i} \[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^{12}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^4 &= 1 
	}
$$

Therefore, to simplify a higher integer power of $\textrm{i},$ we *divide the power by $4$ and raise $\textrm{i}$ to the remainder*.

Let's see this idea in action.
